nodes.name: Base ring Lambda and residue field k
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be a complete Noetherian (commutative) local ring and $k$ its residue field.

nodes.name: Category C_Lambda of Artinian local Lambda-algebras
nodes.statement: We define $\CL$ to be the category of Artinian local $\Lambda$-algebras having residue field $k$, where morphisms are local algebra homomorphisms.
nodes.label: def:ArtinResAlg

nodes.name: Residue field of A
nodes.statement: The condition of having the same residue field for a $\Lambda$-algebra $A$ can be stated in a more general context as follows: the algebra map $\Lambda \to \rf_A$ is surjective (where $\rf_A$ is the residue field of $A$).
nodes.statement_short: Having residue field $k$ means the map $\Lambda \to \rf_A$ is surjective, $\rf_A$ being the residue field of $A$.

nodes.name: Morphisms out of Artinian local rings are local
nodes.statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative local rings, and $f : A \to B$ a ring morphism. If $A$ is Artinian, then $f$ is local.
assumptions: Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative local rings, and $f : A \to B$ a ring morphism.
$A$ is Artinian
nodes.label: lem:islocalhom_of_artinian

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (local hom of Artinian)
nodes.statement: In an Artinian local ring, the maximal ideal is the set of nilpotent elements. In particular if $x \in \m_A$, then $f (x)$ is not a unit.
nodes.statement_short: The maximal ideal of an Artinian local ring is nilpotent, so its image contains no units.

nodes.name: Length over Lambda equals length over A
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a local $\Lambda$-algebra with same residue field as $\Lambda$. Then $\length_\Lambda (A) = \length_A (A)$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a local $\Lambda$-algebra with same residue field as $\Lambda$.
nodes.label: lem:lengtheq

nodes.name: Proof of length equality
nodes.statement: We prove a more general result: if $M$ is an $A$-module, then $\length_\Lambda (M) = \length_A (M)$. This result follows easily by induction on $\length_\Lambda (M)$ from the case $\length_\Lambda (M) = 1$, in which case we have $M \cong k$. \cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06GG}{Tag 06GG}]{stacks-project}
nodes.statement_short: Generalize to $A$-modules and induct on $\Lambda$-length from the simple case $M \cong k$.

nodes.name: C_Lambda has pullbacks
nodes.statement: The category $\CL$ has pullbacks.
nodes.label: lem:has_pullbacks

nodes.name: Proof that C_Lambda has pullbacks
nodes.statement: Let $f : X \to Z$ and $g : Y \to Z$ be morphisms in $\CL$. Consider the set $P = \{(x, y) \in X \times Y ~\vert~ f (x) = g (y)\}$. Since $f$ and $g$ are local, the subset $\m_X \times \m_Y$ is an ideal (which is maximal). We have $\rf_\Lambda \to \rf_P \to \rf_X$, so $\rf_P \cong k$. Furthermore, since $X$ and $Y$ are Artinian $\Lambda$-modules by \cref{lem:lengtheq}, $P$ is an Artinian $\Lambda$-module as well, so it is an Artinian ring.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the fibre product set $P$, check it is local with residue field $k$ and Artinian via length.

nodes.name: k is terminal in C_Lambda; products exist
nodes.statement: We also note that $k$ is a terminal object in $\CL$, so the category also admits products (which are the same as pullbacks over the terminal object).

nodes.name: Surjective morphism p
nodes.statement: Let $p : B \to A$ be a surjective morphism in $\CL$.

nodes.name: Small extension
nodes.statement: $p$ is a \emph{small extension} if $\ker p$ is a non-zero principal ideal such that $\m_B \cdot \ker p = 0$.
differentia: $\ker p$ is a non-zero principal ideal
nodes.label: def:IsSmallExtension

nodes.name: Characterizations of small extensions
nodes.statement: The following propositions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $p$ is a small extension \item $\ker p$ is a minimal non-zero ideal \item $\length_\Lambda (B) = \length_\Lambda (A) + 1$ \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $p : B \to A$ be a surjective morphism in $\CL$.
conclusions: The following propositions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $p$ is a small extension \item $\ker p$ is a minimal non-zero ideal \item $\length_\Lambda (B) = \length_\Lambda (A) + 1$ \end{enumerate}
equivalent_conditions: $\ker p$ is a minimal non-zero ideal
nodes.statement_short: $p$ small extension iff $\ker p$ minimal non-zero iff length of $B$ is length of $A$ plus one.
nodes.label: lem:smallext_iff

nodes.name: Proof of characterizations of small extensions
nodes.statement:
Since $p$ is surjective, we have $\length_\Lambda (B) = \length_\Lambda (A) + \length_\Lambda (\ker p)$, and we also have that $\length_B (\ker p) = 1$ if and only if $\ker p$ is a minimal non-zero ideal, so using \cref{lem:lengtheq} we get $(2) \iff (3)$. We now show $(1) \iff (2)$. Assume that $p$ is a small extension, write $\ker p = (t)$, let $I < \ker p$ be an ideal and $x \in I$. There exists $y \in B$ such that $x = ty$. Since $I 
e (t)$, $y$ is not a unit, so we have $y \in \m_B$, and $x = 0$ by definition of a small extension. So $I=0$ and $\ker p$ is minimal. Assume that $\ker p$ is a minimal non-zero ideal. Let $t \in \ker p \setminus \{0\}$. By minimality, we have $\ker p = (t)$. Furthermore, since $\m_B$ is nilpotent and $\ker p 
eq 0$ we have $\m_B \cdot \ker p 
eq \ker p$ so $\m_B \cdot \ker p = 0$ by minimality. So $p$ is a small extension.
nodes.statement_short: Length additivity gives (2)$\iff$(3); the two directions of (1)$\iff$(2) by direct ideal computations.

nodes.name: Induction principle on surjections via small extensions
nodes.statement: If a property $C$ on morphisms of $\CL$ is satisfied by isomorphisms and stable by composition on the left by a small extension, then it holds for any surjection.
assumptions: a property $C$ on morphisms of $\CL$ is satisfied by isomorphisms and stable by composition on the left by a small extension
nodes.label: lem:smallext_hom_induction

nodes.name: Proof of small extension induction on morphisms
nodes.statement: By induction on $\length_\Lambda (B) \in \N$. If $\ker p = 0$, then $p$ is an isomorphism. Otherwise, there exists a minimal non-zero ideal $I$ of $B$ because $B$ is Artinian. By minimality, since $\ker p \neq 0$, we have $I \le \ker p$, so $p$ factorizes through the small extension $B \to B/I$. We conclude by applying the induction hypothesis to the map $B/I \to A$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the length of $B$, factoring $p$ through a small extension $B \to B/I$ with $I$ minimal.

nodes.name: Induction principle on objects via small extensions
nodes.statement: If a property $C$ on objects of $\CL$ is satisfied by $k$, stable by isomorphisms and stable by small extensions, then it holds for all objects of $\CL$.
assumptions: a property $C$ on objects of $\CL$ is satisfied by $k$, stable by isomorphisms and stable by small extensions
conclusions: it holds for all objects of $\CL$.
nodes.label: lem:smallext_obj_induction

nodes.name: Proof of small extension induction on objects
nodes.statement: One way is to apply the previous lemma to the map $p : B \to k$ (i.e. with the property on morphisms $q : X \to Y$ given by if $Y = k$ then $C (X)$). In the code the proof is essentially copied and adapted from the previous lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the morphism version to $p : B \to k$.

nodes.name: Complete local ring
nodes.statement: A local ring with maximal ideal $\m$ is \emph{complete} if it is $\m$-adically complete.
nodes.label: def:complete

nodes.name: Completed category hat C_Lambda
nodes.statement: We define $\Chat$ to be the category of complete Noetherian local $\Lambda$-algebras having residue field $k$, where morphisms are local algebra homomorphisms.
nodes.label: def:ProArtinResAlg

nodes.name: m-adic topology
nodes.statement: Note that a local ring is endowed with a natural topological ring structure, namely the $\m$-adic topology, where $\m$ is the maximal ideal. It is defined by setting the powers of $\m$ as a neighborhood base of $0$.
differentia: setting the powers of $\m$ as a neighborhood base of $0$

nodes.name: Full subcategory relation between C_Lambda and hat C_Lambda
nodes.statement: The category $\Chat$ is a full subcategory of $\CL$.
conclusions: The category $\Chat$ is a full subcategory of $\CL$.
nodes.label: lem:fullsubcategory

nodes.name: Proof of full subcategory
nodes.statement: An Artinian ring is Noetherian, and its $\m$-adic topology is discrete, so it is trivially complete.
nodes.statement_short: Artinian rings are Noetherian with discrete $\m$-adic topology, hence complete.

nodes.name: Noetherian local ring with nilpotent maximal ideal is Artinian
nodes.statement: A local Noetherian ring whose maximal ideal is nilpotent is Artinian.
assumptions: A local Noetherian ring whose maximal ideal is nilpotent
nodes.label: lem:isArtinian_of_noetherian_nilpotent

nodes.name: Proof of Artinian criterion
nodes.statement: A Noetherian ring is Artinian if and only if it has Krull dimension 0, so it suffices to show that any prime ideal is maximal. Let $I$ be a prime ideal. Since $\m^n = 0 \le I$ we have $\m \le I$, so $I = \m$ is maximal.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Krull dimension 0: a prime containing the nilpotent maximal ideal is maximal.

nodes.name: Quotients by powers of the maximal ideal lie in C_Lambda
nodes.statement: If $A \in \Chat$, then for any $n \in \N^*$ we have $A / \m^n \in \CL$ where $\m$ is the maximal ideal of $A$. In fact, we have $A / J \in \CL$ for any ideal $J$ such that $\m^n \le J < A$.
assumptions: $A \in \Chat$
for any $n \in \N^*$
for any ideal $J$ such that $\m^n \le J < A$
conclusions: $A / \m^n \in \CL$ where $\m$ is the maximal ideal of $A$.

assumptions: for any $n \in \N^*$
conclusions: $A / \m^n \in \CL$ where $\m$ is the maximal ideal of $A$.

assumptions: for any ideal $J$ such that $\m^n \le J < A$

nodes.label: lem:quotinC

nodes.name: Proof that quotients lie in C_Lambda
nodes.statement: $A / \m^n$ is a local Noetherian ring, with nilpotent maximal ideal $\m / \m^n$ and residue field $k$, so \cref{lem:isArtinian_of_noetherian_nilpotent} applies.
nodes.statement_short: The quotient is local Noetherian with nilpotent maximal ideal; apply the Artinian criterion.

nodes.name: Complete ring as inverse limit
nodes.statement: The fact that $A \in \Chat$ is complete (and Noetherian) means that we have $A = \varprojlim A / \m^n$. We don't really use this result here but it explains some of the underlying ideas.
nodes.statement_short: Completeness of $A \in \Chat$ means $A = \varprojlim A/\m^n$; not used, only explanatory.

nodes.name: Maps from hat C_Lambda to C_Lambda factor through a finite quotient
nodes.statement: Let $R \in \Chat$, $A \in \CL$ and $u : R \to A$. There exists $n \in \N^*$ such that $\m_R^n \le \ker u$, so $u$ factorizes through $u_n : R/\m_R^n \to A$.
assumptions: Let $R \in \Chat$, $A \in \CL$ and $u : R \to A$.
conclusions: There exists $n \in \N^*$ such that $\m_R^n \le \ker u$, so $u$ factorizes through $u_n : R/\m_R^n \to A$.
nodes.label: lem:factorizes

nodes.name: Proof of factorization
nodes.statement: There exists $n$ such that $\m_A^n = 0$, so $\m_R^n \le u^{-1} (\m_A ^n) = \ker u$.
nodes.statement_short: $\m_A$ is nilpotent, so a power of $\m_R$ maps to zero.

nodes.name: Trivial square-zero extension k[V]
nodes.statement: For $V$ a $k$-vector space, we write $k[V]$ for the \emph{trivial square-zero extension} of $V$ over $k$, that is the module $k \oplus V$ with multiplication defined so that $V ^ 2 = 0$.
nodes.label: def:tsze_C

nodes.name: Dual numbers k[epsilon]
nodes.statement: We write $k[\varepsilon]$ for \emph{dual numbers}, the special case where $V = k$.
nodes.label: def:dualnumber_C

nodes.name: Trivial square-zero extension functor
nodes.statement: We can a functor $\Mod_k^{fg} \to \CL$ that commutes with finite products (where $\Mod_k^{fg}$ is the category of finite dimensional $k$-vector spaces).
nodes.statement_short: The construction $V \mapsto k[V]$ is a functor from finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces to $\CL$ commuting with finite products.
nodes.label: def:tsze_functor

nodes.name: Vector space structure on F(k[V])
nodes.statement: If $F$ is a functor $\CL \to Sets$ such that \[ F(k[V] \times k[W]) ~ \tilde{\to} ~ F(k[V]) \times F(k[W]) \] for all finite dimensional $k$-vector spaces $V$ and $W$, then $F(k[V])$ has a canonical $k$-vector space structure.
assumptions: $F$ is a functor $\CL \to Sets$ such that \[ F(k[V] \times k[W]) ~ \tilde{\to} ~ F(k[V]) \times F(k[W]) \] for all finite dimensional $k$-vector spaces $V$ and $W$
nodes.label: lem:vstsze

nodes.name: Proof of vector space structure on F(k[V])
nodes.statement: This is a special case of the following lemma \cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/06I6}{Tag 06I6}]{stacks-project}:
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the module-structure lemma for product-preserving functors (Stacks 06I6).

nodes.name: Product-preserving functors on modules carry module structures
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a (commutative) ring, and $L : \Mod_R^{fg} \to Sets$ be a functor that preserves finite products. Then for any $M \in \Mod_R^{fg}$, $L(M)$ has a canonical $R$-module structure.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a (commutative) ring, and $L : \Mod_R^{fg} \to Sets$ be a functor that preserves finite products.
conclusions: for any $M \in \Mod_R^{fg}$, $L(M)$ has a canonical $R$-module structure.
nodes.label: lem:vs

nodes.name: Proof of module structure on L(M)
nodes.statement: Let $M \in \Mod_R^{fg}$. Write $s : M \times M \to M$ for the addition map, $\lambda_r : M \to M$ for the scalar multiplication by $r \in R$, and $z : 0 \to M$. The module structure on $L(M)$ is defined using the images of these morphisms by $L$, together with the identification $L(M\times M) \cong L(M) \times L(M)$, and the fact that $L(0)$ is terminal in $Sets$ so it is a singleton. Checking that this defines a module structure is rather straightforward, by writing suitable commutative diagrams in $\Mod_R^{fg}$ and pushing them with $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport addition, scalar multiplication and zero maps through $L$ using $L(M\times M) \cong L(M)\times L(M)$.

nodes.name: Natural transformations are linear
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a (commutative) ring, $L$ and $L' : \Mod_R^{fg} \to Sets$ be two functors that preserve finite products, and $\eta : L \to L'$ a natural transformation. Then for any $M \in \Mod_R^{fg}$, $\eta_M$ is $R$-linear.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a (commutative) ring, $L$ and $L' : \Mod_R^{fg} \to Sets$ be two functors that preserve finite products, and $\eta : L \to L'$ a natural transformation.
nodes.label: lem:vsnatlin

nodes.name: Proof of linearity
nodes.statement: This is a very simple check.

nodes.name: Natural isomorphism criterion on R
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a (commutative) ring, $L$ and $L' : \Mod_R^{fg} \to Sets$ be two functors that preserve finite products, and $\eta : L \to L'$ a natural transformation. Then $\eta$ is an isomorphism if and only if $\eta_R$ is an isomorphism.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a (commutative) ring, $L$ and $L' : \Mod_R^{fg} \to Sets$ be two functors that preserve finite products, and $\eta : L \to L'$ a natural transformation.
conclusions: $\eta$ is an isomorphism if and only if $\eta_R$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.label: lem:vsnatiso

nodes.name: Proof of isomorphism criterion
nodes.statement: By induction on the dimension.

nodes.name: Hom functor h_R
nodes.statement: For $R \in \Chat$ and $A \in \CL$, we define a functor $\CL \to Sets$ by $h_R (A) = \Hom_{\Chat}(R, A)$.
nodes.label: def:hR

nodes.name: Functors preserve terminal objects
nodes.statement: In what follows we will only consider functors $F$ from $\CL$ to $Sets$ that preserve terminal objects, or equivalently such that $F(k)$ is a singleton.

nodes.name: Completion hat F of a functor
nodes.statement: We can extend such a functor to $\Chat$ by setting for $R \in \Chat$, $\hat{F}(R) = \varprojlim F(R / \m^n)$. A map $u : R \to S$ induces maps $u_n : R / \m_R^n \to S / \m_S^n$ for all $n \in \N$, so we can also define $\hat{F}(u)$ by using the universal property. This defines a functor $\hat{F} : \Chat \to Sets$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend $F$ to $\Chat$ by $\hat F(R) = \varprojlim F(R/\m^n)$, with maps induced by the universal property.
nodes.label: def:completion

nodes.name: Restriction of hat F to C_Lambda is F
nodes.statement: There is a natural isomorphism $\hat{F}\restr{\CL} \cong F$.
conclusions: There is a natural isomorphism $\hat{F}\restr{\CL} \cong F$.
nodes.label: lem:isocompl

nodes.name: Proof of restriction isomorphism
nodes.statement: If $A$ is in $\CL$, there exists $N \in \N^*$ such that $\m_A^N=0$, so we have $F(A/\m_A^n) \cong F(A)$ for all $n \ge N$.
nodes.statement_short: For $A \in \CL$ the inverse system $F(A/\m_A^n)$ is eventually constant.

nodes.name: Pro-couple
nodes.statement: A \emph{pro-couple} is a pair $(R, \xi)$ where $R \in \Chat$ and $\xi \in \hat{F} (R)$.
nodes.label: def:procouple

nodes.name: Natural transformation induced by a pro-couple
nodes.statement: A pro-couple $(R, \xi)$ defines a natural transformation $\nattrans(\xi) : h_R \to F$ given by $u \mapsto \hat{F} (u) (\xi)$ up to the isomorphism given in lemma~\ref{lem:isocompl}.
nodes.statement_short: A pro-couple $(R,\xi)$ gives $h_R \to F$, $u \mapsto \hat F(u)(\xi)$, via $\hat F|_{\CL} \cong F$.
nodes.label: def:nattrans_of

nodes.name: Compatibility of nattrans with composition
nodes.statement: Let $(R, \xi)$ be a pro-couple, $A, B \in \CL$, $u : R \to A$ and $v : A \to B$. Then $\nattrans(\xi) (v \circ u) = F(v)(\nattrans(\xi) (u))$.
assumptions: Let $(R, \xi)$ be a pro-couple, $A, B \in \CL$, $u : R \to A$ and $v : A \to B$.
nodes.label: lem:nattrans_of_comp_artinhom

nodes.name: Proof of compatibility with composition
nodes.statement: This is essentially the naturality of $\hat{F}\restr{\CL} \cong F$.

nodes.name: nattrans of a quotient map is the component
nodes.statement: Let $(R, \xi)$ be a pro-couple, with $\xi = (\xi_q)_{q\in\N}$, $n\in\N^*$, and $p:R\to R/\m_R^n$ the quotient map. Then $\nattrans(\xi) (p) = \xi_n$.
assumptions: Let $(R, \xi)$ be a pro-couple, with $\xi = (\xi_q)_{q\in\N}$, $n\in\N^*$, and $p:R\to R/\m_R^n$ the quotient map.
nodes.label: lem:completion_map_quot_mk_eq_pi

nodes.name: Proof for quotient maps
nodes.statement: In fact, we have that $\hat{F}(p)$ is equal to the projection $\hat{F}(R) \to F(R / \m_R^n)$ composed with the natural isomorphism $F \cong \hat{F}\restr{\CL}$. This is a simple check.
nodes.statement_short: $\hat F(p)$ is the projection to $F(R/\m_R^n)$ composed with $F \cong \hat F|_{\CL}$.

nodes.name: nattrans via finite quotients
nodes.statement: In particular, since any map $R \to A$ with $A \in \CL$ factorizes through some $u_n : R / \m^n \to A$ (\cref{lem:factorizes}), we have $\nattrans(\xi) (u) = F(u_n) (\xi_n)$.
assumptions: any map $R \to A$ with $A \in \CL$ factorizes through some $u_n : R / \m^n \to A$

nodes.name: Pro-representability
nodes.statement: A pro-couple $(R, \xi)$ \emph{pro-represents} $F$ if the natural transformation $\nattrans(\xi) : h_R \to F$ it induces is an isomorphism. $F$ is \emph{pro-representable} if there exists a pro-couple which pro-represents $F$.
nodes.statement_short: $(R,\xi)$ pro-represents $F$ if $h_R \to F$ is an isomorphism; $F$ is pro-representable if such a pro-couple exists.
nodes.label: def:Prorepresents

nodes.name: Smooth natural transformation
nodes.statement: Let $F, G : \CL \to Sets$ be two functors that preserve terminal objects. A natural transformation $\eta : F \to G$ is \emph{smooth} if for any surjection $p : B \to A$ in $\CL$, the morphism \[ F(B) \to F(A) \times_{G(A)} G(B)\] is surjective.
differentia: for any surjection $p : B \to A$ in $\CL$, the morphism \[ F(B) \to F(A) \times_{G(A)} G(B)\] is surjective.
nodes.label: def:IsSmooth

nodes.name: Smoothness can be checked on small extensions
nodes.statement: To check that a natural transformation is smooth, it is enough to check the condition on morphisms $p$ that are small extensions.
conclusions: To check that a natural transformation is smooth, it is enough to check the condition on morphisms $p$ that are small extensions.
nodes.label: lem:smoothsmallext

nodes.name: Proof of smoothness on small extensions
nodes.statement: Apply \cref{lem:smallext_hom_induction}. Check that the property is stable by composition (note that the pullback is in $Sets$).
nodes.statement_short: Apply the small-extension induction on surjections; the lifting property is stable under composition.

nodes.name: Smooth transformations are surjective
nodes.statement: Let $F, G : \CL \to Sets$ be two functors that preserve terminal objects. If $\eta : F \to G$ is smooth, then $\eta_A$ is surjective for any $A \in \CL$.
assumptions: Let $F, G : \CL \to Sets$ be two functors that preserve terminal objects.
$\eta : F \to G$ is smooth
nodes.label: lem:surj_of_smooth

nodes.name: Proof of surjectivity of smooth maps
nodes.statement: Apply the condition to $p : A \to k$ (using that $F(k)$ and $G(k)$ are singletons).
nodes.statement_short: Apply smoothness to $A \to k$, using that $F(k)$ and $G(k)$ are singletons.

nodes.name: Tangent space t_F
nodes.statement: The \emph{tangent space} of a functor $F$ is $t_F = F(k[\varepsilon])$. In the case $F = h_R$, we simply write $t_R$.
nodes.label: def:tangentSpace

nodes.name: Hull
nodes.statement: A pro-couple $(R, \xi)$ is a \emph{hull} of $F$ if the natural transformation $\nattrans(\xi) : h_R \to F$ it induces is smooth and $\nattrans(\xi)_{k[\varepsilon]} : t_R \to t_F$ is an isomorphism.
differentia: $\nattrans(\xi) : h_R \to F$ it induces is smooth
nodes.label: def:IsHull

nodes.name: Isomorphism on dual numbers extends to k[V]
nodes.statement: Note that if $\eta : F \to G$ is an isomorphism on $k[\varepsilon]$, then it is an isomorphism on $k[V]$ for any finite dimensional $k$-vector space (lemma~\ref{lem:vsnatiso}).
assumptions: $\eta : F \to G$ is an isomorphism on $k[\varepsilon]$
conclusions: it is an isomorphism on $k[V]$ for any finite dimensional $k$-vector space

nodes.name: Functor F with F(k) a singleton
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a functor from $\CL$ to $Sets$ such that $F(k)$ is a singleton.
also_stated_at: Let $F$ be a functor from $\CL$ to $Sets$ such that $F(k)$ is a singleton.

nodes.name: Comparison morphism p_{f,g}
nodes.statement: For $f : X \to Z$ and $G : Y \to Z$ morphisms in $\CL$, we consider the comparison morphism: \begin{equation} p_{f, g} : F(X \times_Z Y) \to F(X) \times_{F(Z)} F(Y) \end{equation}

nodes.name: Comparison morphism
nodes.statement: p_{f, g} : F(X \times_Z Y) \to F(X) \times_{F(Z)} F(Y)
nodes.label: eq:pfg

nodes.name: Schlessinger condition (H1)
nodes.statement: $(H_1)$ : if $g$ is a small extension then $p_{f, g}$ is surjective.
nodes.label: def:H1

nodes.name: Schlessinger condition (H2)
nodes.statement: $(H_2)$ : if $Z = k$ and $Y = k[\varepsilon]$ then $p_{f, g}$ is bijective.
nodes.label: def:H2

nodes.name: Schlessinger condition (H3)
nodes.statement: $(H_3)$ : assuming $(H_2)$, $\dim_k (t_F) < \infty$.
nodes.label: def:H3

nodes.name: Schlessinger condition (H4)
nodes.statement: $(H_4)$ : if $f$ is a small extension then $p_{f, f}$ is bijective.
nodes.label: def:H4

nodes.name: Conditions quantify over all morphisms
nodes.statement: These conditions are on the functor $F$, so for example "$F$ satisfies $(H_1)$" means that for any morphisms $f$ and $g$, if $g$ is a small extension, then $p_{f, g}$ is surjective.

nodes.name: (H2) gives a vector space structure on t_F
nodes.statement: The definition of $(H_3)$ makes sense because the condition $(H_2)$ implies that $F$ verifies the hypothesis of lemma~\ref{lem:vstsze}, so that $t_F$ admits a canonical $k$-vector space structure.
assumptions: the condition $(H_2)$
conclusions: $F$ verifies the hypothesis of lemma~\ref{lem:vstsze}, so that $t_F$ admits a canonical $k$-vector space structure.
nodes.label: lem:vsh2

nodes.name: (H2) extends to products with k[V]
nodes.statement: If $F$ satisfies $(H_2)$, we have $F(A \times k[V]) \cong F(A) \times F(k[V])$ for any $A \in \CL$ and any $V \in \Mod_k^{fg}$.
assumptions: $F$ satisfies $(H_2)$
for any $A \in \CL$ and any $V \in \Mod_k^{fg}$
nodes.label: lem:h2+

nodes.name: Proof of (H2) extension
nodes.statement: By induction on the dimension of $V$.

nodes.name: (H1) extends to all surjections
nodes.statement: If $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, then $p_{f, g}$ is surjective for any surjection $g$.
assumptions: $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$
conclusions: $p_{f, g}$ is surjective for any surjection $g$.
nodes.label: lem:h1+

nodes.name: Proof of (H1) extension
nodes.statement: A surjection $g$ is either an isomorphism or it can be factored as a composition of small extensions. The result is clear for isomorphisms and we can show that if $g_1$ and $g_2$ are two suitable morphisms such that $p_{f, g_1}$ and $p_{f, g_2}$ are surjective then $p_{f, g_2 \circ g_1}$ is surjective as well.
nodes.statement_short: Factor a surjection into small extensions and show surjectivity of $p_{f,g}$ is stable under composition.

nodes.name: h_R satisfies Schlessinger's conditions
nodes.statement: The functor $h_R$ satisfies conditions $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$, $(H_3)$ and $(H_4)$.
nodes.label: lem:hRconds

nodes.name: Proof that h_R satisfies (H1)-(H4)
nodes.statement: In fact in this case $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$ and $(H_4)$ hold trivially since $p_{f, g}$ is an isomorphism for any morphisms $f$ and $g$, because $h_R$ is a hom-functor, and pullbacks in $\CL$ are pullbacks in $\Chat$. For $(H_3)$, it suffices to show the following linear isomorphism $t_R^* \cong \m_R / (\m_R ^ 2 + \m_\Lambda R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hom-functors turn pullbacks into products, so $p_{f,g}$ is an isomorphism; (H3) via $t_R^* \cong \m_R/(\m_R^2+\m_\Lambda R)$.

nodes.name: Schlessinger's theorem (existence of a hull)
nodes.statement: If $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$ and $(H_3)$, then $F$ admits a hull.
assumptions: $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$ and $(H_3)$
nodes.label: thm:Schlessinger1

nodes.name: Schlessinger's theorem (necessity of conditions for a hull)
nodes.statement: If $F$ admits a hull, then $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$ and $(H_3)$.
assumptions: $F$ admits a hull
nodes.label: thm:Schlessinger2

nodes.name: Schlessinger's theorem (pro-representability)
nodes.statement: If $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$, $(H_3)$ and $(H_4)$, then $F$ is pro-representable.
nodes.label: thm:Schlessinger3

nodes.name: Schlessinger's theorem (necessity for pro-representability)
nodes.statement: If $F$ is pro-representable, then $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$, $(H_3)$ and $(H_4)$.
assumptions: $F$ is pro-representable
nodes.label: thm:Schlessinger4

nodes.name: Proof of necessity for pro-representability
nodes.statement: $h_R$ satisfies all four conditions as noted in \cref{lem:hRconds}, so this is trivial (using \cref{lem:vsnatlin} for $(H_3)$).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $h_R$, which satisfies all four conditions; linearity lemma for (H3).

nodes.name: Essential surjection
nodes.statement: A surjective morphism $p : B \to A$ in $\CL$ is \emph{essential} if for any morphism $q : C \to B$ such that $q \circ p$ is surjective, $q$ is surjective.
differentia: for any morphism $q : C \to B$ such that $q \circ p$ is surjective, $q$ is surjective.
nodes.label: def:IsEssential

nodes.name: Essential surjections test maps from hat C_Lambda
nodes.statement: Let $p : B \to A$ be essential and $q : C \to B$ be a morphism in $\Chat$ such that $q \circ p$ is surjective. Then $q$ is surjective.
assumptions: Let $p : B \to A$ be essential and $q : C \to B$ be a morphism in $\Chat$ such that $q \circ p$ is surjective.
nodes.label: lem:essential_proartin

nodes.name: Proof for essential maps from hat C_Lambda
nodes.statement: This is trivial considering that $q$ factorizes through $q_n : C/\m_C^n \to B$ for some $n$ which is a morphism in $\CL$ (\cref{lem:factorizes}).
nodes.statement_short: Factor $q$ through a finite quotient in $\CL$ and apply the definition.

nodes.name: Non-essential small extensions split
nodes.statement: If $p : B \to A$ is a small extension, then $p$ is not essential if and only if $p$ admits a section, that is there exists a morphism $s : A \to B$ such that $p \circ s = \mathbb{1}_A$.
assumptions: $p : B \to A$ is a small extension
conclusions: $p$ is not essential if and only if $p$ admits a section, that is there exists a morphism $s : A \to B$ such that $p \circ s = \mathbb{1}_A$.
equivalent_conditions: $p$ admits a section, that is there exists a morphism $s : A \to B$ such that $p \circ s = \mathbb{1}_A$.
nodes.label: lem:14ii

nodes.name: Proof that non-essential small extensions split
nodes.statement: If $p$ has a section $s$, then $p$ is not essential since $s$ is not surjective as we have $\length_\Lambda (B) = \length_\Lambda (A) + 1$. Now, suppose that $p$ is not essential, and let $q : C \to B$ be such that $q \circ p$ is surjective but $q$ is not. Let $C'$ be the range of $q$. We have $\length_\Lambda (C') < \length_\Lambda (B)$ since $q$ is not surjective so $\length_\Lambda (C') \le \length_\Lambda (A)$, and $\length_\Lambda (C') \ge \length_\Lambda (A)$ because $p\restr{C'}$ is surjective (because $q \circ p$ is). Thus $p\restr{C'}$ is bijective which gives the section that we wanted.
nodes.statement_short: Length counting: a section is not surjective; conversely the image of a non-surjective $q$ maps bijectively onto $A$.

nodes.name: Small extension p with kernel I
nodes.statement: Let $p : B \to A$ be a small extension in $\CL$, and write $I = \ker p$.

nodes.name: B x k[I] is isomorphic to B x_A B
nodes.statement: There is an isomorphism $B \times k[I] \cong B \times_A B$ whose first component is the identity.
conclusions: There is an isomorphism $B \times k[I] \cong B \times_A B$ whose first component is the identity.
nodes.label: lem:isosmallext

nodes.name: Proof of the isomorphism B x k[I] = B x_A B
nodes.statement: It is given by $(x, r + y) \mapsto (x, x + y)$. The inverse map is $(x, y) \mapsto (x, x_0 + y - x)$ where $x_0$ is the $k$ residue of $x$. It is easy to check that this defines an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit map $(x, r+y) \mapsto (x, x+y)$ with explicit inverse.

nodes.name: Action of F(k[I]) on F(B)
nodes.statement: Let $F : \CL \to Sets$ such that $F(k)$ is a singleton and $F$ satisfies $(H_2)$. Using the isomorphism from lemma~\ref{lem:isosmallext} together with the comparison maps (\cref{eq:pfg}), we get a map $$F(B) \times F(k[I]) \to F(B) \times_{F(A)} F(B)$$ This defines an action of $F(k[I])$ on $F(B)$, with orbits contained in the fibers of $p$.
assumptions: Let $F : \CL \to Sets$ such that $F(k)$ is a singleton and $F$ satisfies $(H_2)$.
conclusions: This defines an action of $F(k[I])$ on $F(B)$, with orbits contained in the fibers of $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Under (H2), the isomorphism $B\times k[I]\cong B\times_A B$ yields an action of $F(k[I])$ on $F(B)$ preserving fibres of $p$.
nodes.label: lem:action

nodes.name: Proof of the action
nodes.statement: This is simply a formal check. In practice we only need the fact that $0$ acts trivially, so there is less to check.
nodes.statement_short: Formal check; only triviality of the $0$ action is needed.

nodes.name: (H1) gives transitive action on fibres
nodes.statement: The condition $(H_1)$ implies that the map in \cref{lem:action} is surjective, i.e. the action is transitive on fibers of $p$.
assumptions: The condition $(H_1)$
conclusions: the map in \cref{lem:action} is surjective, i.e. the action is transitive on fibers of $p$.
nodes.label: lem:actionH1

nodes.name: (H4) gives principal homogeneous fibres
nodes.statement: The condition $(H_4)$ implies that the map in \cref{lem:action} is bijective, i.e. the fibers of $p$ are principal homogeneous spaces under $F(k[I])$.
assumptions: The condition $(H_4)$
conclusions: the map in \cref{lem:action} is bijective, i.e. the fibers of $p$ are principal homogeneous spaces under $F(k[I])$.
nodes.label: lem:actionH4

nodes.name: Functoriality of the action
nodes.statement: The action defined in \cref{lem:action} is functorial: if $G$ is another functor with the necessary conditions, and $\eta : F \to G$ is a natural transformation, then the following diagram commutes: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} {G(B) \times G(k[I])} \arrow[rr] & & G(B) \times_{G(A)} G(B) \\ {F(B) \times F(k[I])} \arrow[rr] \arrow[u] & & F(B) \times_{F(A)} F(B) \arrow[u] \end{tikzcd} \end{center}
assumptions: $G$ is another functor with the necessary conditions, and $\eta : F \to G$ is a natural transformation
conclusions: The action defined in \cref{lem:action} is functorial
nodes.label: lem:actionnattrans

nodes.name: Decreasing ideals define the adic topology on R/J
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be an object of $\Chat$, and let $(J_n)_{n\in\N}$ be a decreasing sequence of ideals of $R$ such that $\m_R^n \le J_n$. Set $J = \bigcap_{n\in\N} J_n$. Then the sequence $(J_n/J)_{n\in\N}$ defines the $\m_{R/J}$-adic topology on $R/J$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be an object of $\Chat$, and let $(J_n)_{n\in\N}$ be a decreasing sequence of ideals of $R$ such that $\m_R^n \le J_n$.
Set $J = \bigcap_{n\in\N} J_n$.
conclusions: the sequence $(J_n/J)_{n\in\N}$ defines the $\m_{R/J}$-adic topology on $R/J$.
nodes.label: lem:topo

nodes.name: Proof of the topology lemma
nodes.statement: We need to show that for any $n \in \N$, there exists $N\in\N$ such that $J_N \le J + \m_R^n$. For every $k \in \N$, $R / \m_R^k$ is Artinian, so the decreasing sequence $(J_i + \m_R^k)_{i \in \N}$ stabilizes. We write $N_k$ for some index such that $J_{N_k} + \m_R^k$ is the minimum of the sequence. Note that we have $J_{N_k} + \m_R^k \le J_k + \m_R^k$ so since we also have $\m_R^k \le J_k$ we get that $J_{N_k} \le J_k$. We claim that $J_{N_n} \le J + \m_R^n$. Let $x \in J_{N_n}$. We define a Cauchy sequence $(x_i)$ in $R$ with $x_i \in J_{N_i}$ for $i \ge n$ by induction, by first setting $x_i = x$ if $i \le n$. If $i > n$, then there exists $x_{i+1} \in J_{N_{i+1}}$ such that $x_i - x_{i+1} \in \m_R ^ i$: indeed if $N_{i+1} \le N_i$ we can take $x_{i+1}= x_i$, and otherwise we have $J_{N_{i+1}} + \m_R^i = J_{N_i} + \m_R^i$ (note that have $x_i \in J_{N_i}$). Since $R$ is complete, this sequence admits a limit $y$. We have $y \in J_{N_i} + \m_R^i$ for all $i$ so $y \in J$ and $y - x = y - x_n \in \m_R ^ n$, so $x \in J + \m_R^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Artinian stabilization of $J_i + \m_R^k$, then build a Cauchy sequence. The key step is the limit $y \in J$ obtained by completeness of $R$.

nodes.name: hat F of R/J as an inverse limit over J_n
nodes.statement: In particular, this means that if $J \ne R$, we have $\hat{F}(R/J) \cong \varprojlim F(R / J_n)$.
assumptions: $J \ne R$

nodes.name: Proof of existence of a hull
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$ and $(H_3)$. Let $r = \dim_k(t_F)$, $S = \Lambda[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]$ and $
$ the maximal ideal of $S$. We first construct $R$ as a projective limit of quotients of $S$. More specifically we define a sequence $(J_q, \xi_q)_{q\ge2}$ by induction where $(J_q)$ is a decreasing sequence of ideals of $S$ such that $R_q = S / J_q \in \CL$ and $\xi_q \in F(R_q)$ is such that $(\xi_q) \in \varprojlim F(R_q)$. First we set $J_2 = 
^2 + \m_\Lambda S$ and $R_2 = S/J_2$. There exists $\xi_2 \in R_2$ inducing an isomorphism $\Hom (R_2, k[\varepsilon]) \cong t_F$. To see this, first note that $R_2 \cong k[k^r] \cong k[\varepsilon]^r$. By applying $(H_2)$, this yields $F(R_2) \cong t_F^r$, so choosing a basis $(e_1, \ldots, e_r)$ of $t_F$ gives an element $\xi_2 \in F(R_2)$. We then check that $u \mapsto F(u)(\xi_2)$ is an isomorphism. In fact, this map is linear and sends the morphism $R_2 	o k[\varepsilon]$ corresponding to the $i$-th projection $k^r 	o k$ to $e_i$. For the induction step, suppose that we have an ideal $J_q$ such that $R_q = S/J_q \in \CL$ and $\xi_q \in F(R_q)$. Consider the set $\mathscr{S}$ of ideals $J$ of $S$ such that $
 J_q \le J \le J_q$ and $\xi_q$ lifts to $F(S/J)$. We will set $J_{q+1}$ to be the minimum of $\mathscr{S}$, with $\xi_{q+1}$ some lift of $\xi_q$, after proving that it exists. First note that $\mathscr{S}$ is not empty as it contains $J_q$, and since $S / 
 J_q$ is Artinian, we know that $\mathscr{S}$ admits a minimal element, so we only need to show that $\mathscr{S}$ is stable by pairwise intersection to get a minimum. Let $J$ and $K$ be two elements of $\mathscr{S}$. The elements of $\mathscr{S}$ are in correspondence with $k$-vector subspaces of $J/
 J_q$, so we can extend $J$ into some ideal $J' \le J_q$ such that $J' \cap K = J \cap K$ and $J' + K = J_q$, and we have $J' \in \mathscr{S}$ because $J \le J'$. We now use the isomorphism $$S/J' 	imes_{S/J_q} S/K \cong S/(J \cap K)$$ together with \cref{lem:h1+} to conclude that $\xi_q$ lifts to $S/(J \cap K)$, i.e. that $J \cap K \in \mathscr{S}$, which concludes the induction step. We set $J =  igcap_{q \ge 2} J_q$ and $R = S / J$. By definition of the $J_q$'s, we have $
 ^ q \le J_q$, so \cref{lem:topo} applies and $\hat{F}(R) = \varprojlim F(S/J_q)$, so we can set $\xi = \varprojlim \xi_q \in \hat{F}(R)$. We have $\Hom (R, k[\varepsilon]) \cong \Hom (R_2, k[\varepsilon])$ because any map $S 	o k[\varepsilon]$ factorizes through $S/J_2$, and since $\xi$ projects to $\xi_2$ we have $t_R \cong t_F$ by definition of $\xi_2$. It remains to show that $
attrans(\xi) : h_R 	o F$ is smooth. Using \cref{lem:smoothsmallext}, let $p : A' 	o A$ be a small extension, $u : R 	o A$, $\eta' \in F(A')$ and $\eta \in F(A)$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u) = F(p)(\eta') = \eta$. We need to find $u' : R 	o A'$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u') = \eta'$ and $p \circ u' = u$. First we reduce this to finding $u'' : R 	o A'$ such that $p \circ u'' = u$. Indeed, if we have such a $u''$, then $
attrans(\xi) (u'')$ and $\eta'$ both lie over $\eta$, so by \cref{lem:actionH1}, there exists $\sigma \in F(k[I])$ sending $
attrans(\xi) (u'')$ to $\eta'$, where $I = \ker p$. By using \cref{lem:actionnattrans} and the fact that $h_R (k[I]) \cong F(k[I])$ (using \cref{lem:vsnatiso}), we can also apply $\sigma$ to $u''$ giving us the $u' : R 	o A'$ that we wanted. Since $u$ factorizes through $R/\m_R^n 	o A$ for some $n$, and the topology is induced by the $J_q$'s (\cref{lem:topo}), $u$ factorizes through $R_q 	o A$ for some $q$. It suffices to find $v$ completing the following diagram:  egin{center}  egin{tikzcd} S \arrow[rr, "w"] \arrow[d] & & R_q 	imes_A A' \arrow[d, "pr_1"] \ R_{q+1} \arrow[rr] \arrow[rru, "v", dashed] & & R_q \end{tikzcd} \end{center} where $w$ is defined using the universal property of $S = \Lambda [[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]$ to make the diagram commute. More specifically, to define $w$ we use that $pr_1$ is surjective so that we can first define $w$ on the $X_i$'s, and since all maps are local the images of the $X_i$'s are in the maximal ideal so we can extend the map to $S$. In this context we can easily show that $pr_1$ is a small extension, so we can apply \cref{lem:14ii}. If $pr_1$ admits a section then we are done. Otherwise, $pr_1$ is essential, and $pr_1 \circ w$ is the quotient map $S 	o R_q$, so $w$ is surjective by \cref{lem:essential_proartin}. By $(H_1)$, $\xi_q$ lifts to $R_q 	imes_A A'$, so $\ker w \in \mathscr{S}$ and by minimality we have $J_{q+1} \le \ker w$. Thus $w$ factors through $R_{q+1}$ giving the $v$ that we wanted.
nodes.statement_short: Build $R = S/\bigcap J_q$ by inductively choosing minimal ideals $J_{q+1}$ over which $\xi_q$ lifts, then verify the hull properties. Smoothness reduces via essential small extensions and minimality of $J_{q+1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of necessity of conditions for a hull
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $F$ admits a hull $(R, \xi)$. First since $t_R \cong t_F$ (linearly by \cref{lem:vsnatlin}), and $h_R$ satisfies $(H_3)$, $F$ satisfies $(H_3)$. To check $(H_1)$, let $f : X 	o Z$ and $g : Y 	o Z$ be morphisms in $\CL$ with $g$ surjective, and $x \in F(X)$ and $y \in F(Y)$ both lying over $z \in F(Z)$. First, since $h_R 	o F$ is smooth, by \cref{lem:surj_of_smooth} there exists $u_x : R 	o X$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u_x) = x$. Then by smoothness applied to $g$, there exists $u_y : R 	o Y$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u_y) = y$ and $g \circ u_y = f \circ u_x$. Then $
attrans(\xi)(u_x 	imes u_y) \in F(X 	imes_Z Y)$ projects to $x$ and $y$, so $p_{f, g}$ is surjective. To check $(H_2)$, we now only need to check injectivity, since we have already shown $(H_1)$. Let $A \in \CL$ and $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ in $F(A 	imes k[\varepsilon])$ having the same projections $a \in F(A)$ and $e \in k[\varepsilon]$. We proceed similarly as in the proof of $(H_1)$. First there is $u' : R 	o A$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u') = a$. Then by smoothness applied to the projection $pr_1 : A 	imes k[\varepsilon] 	o A$, we get maps $u_i : R 	o A 	imes k[\varepsilon]$ for $i = 1, 2$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u_i) = \zeta_i$ and $pr_1 \circ u_i = u'$. Since $
attrans(\xi) (pr_2 \circ u_i) = e$ in both cases, and $
attrans(\xi)_{k[\varepsilon]}$ is an isomorphism, we have $u_1 = u_2$ so $\zeta_1 = \zeta_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift elements along a smooth $h_R \to F$ and transfer (H1), (H2), (H3) from $h_R$.

nodes.name: Proof of pro-representability
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$, $(H_3)$ and $(H_4)$. By the first point of the theorem, we know that $F$ admits a hull $(R, \xi)$. Furthermore, since $
attrans(\xi)$ is smooth, we already know that $
attrans(\xi)_A$ is surjective for all $A \in \CL$ (\cref{lem:surj_of_smooth}). We will show by induction on $\length_\Lambda (A)$ that it is injective, using \cref{lem:smallextexist}. If $A = k$, then this is true by definition of a hull. Otherwise, let $p : B 	o A$ be a small extension, with $I = \ker p$, and suppose that $
attrans(\xi)_A$ is an isomorphism. By applying \cref{lem:actionH4} together with \cref{lem:actionnattrans}, it is easy check that $
attrans(\xi)_B$ is injective. Namely we take $u_1$ and $u_2$ in $h_R(B)$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u_1) = 
attrans(\xi) (u_2)$, and we need to show that the action of $h_R(k[I])$ by $0$ sends $u_1$ to $u_2$, which is clear from the commutative diagram in \cref{lem:actionnattrans}.
nodes.statement_short: Take a hull and prove injectivity of $h_R \to F$ by induction on length using small extensions and the (H4) action.

nodes.name: Hilbert basis theorem for power series
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring. Then $R[[X]]$ is Noetherian.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring.
nodes.label: lem:powerseriesnoetherian

nodes.name: Membership in powers of the maximal ideal of a power series ring
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a local ring, $\m$ its maximal ideal, $r, k \in \N$, $\n$ the maximal ideal of $R[[X_1, \cdots , X_r]]$ and $x = (x_n)_{n \in \N ^ {r}} \in R[[X_1, \cdots , X_r]]$. Then $x \in \n ^ k \iff \forall n \in \N ^ {r}, x_n \in \m ^ {k - \deg (n)}$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a local ring, $\m$ its maximal ideal, $r, k \in \N$, $\n$ the maximal ideal of $R[[X_1, \cdots , X_r]]$ and $x = (x_n)_{n \in \N ^ {r}} \in R[[X_1, \cdots , X_r]]$.
nodes.label: lem:mem_maximalideal_pow

nodes.name: Proof sketch for power series membership
nodes.statement: The forward direction is easy. The converse should probably be shown by induction on $r$ (and $k$).
nodes.statement_short: Forward direction easy; converse by induction on $r$ and $k$ (sketch).

nodes.name: h_R preserves pullbacks
nodes.statement: The functor $h_R$ (see \cref{def:hR}) preserves pullbacks.
nodes.label: lem:preservesPullbackshR

nodes.name: Proof that h_R preserves pullbacks
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that the inclusion functor preserves pullbacks.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the inclusion functor preserving pullbacks.

nodes.name: h_R satisfies (H3)
nodes.statement: The functor $h_R$ satisfies $(H_3)$.
nodes.label: lem:H3hR

nodes.name: Partial proof that h_R satisfies (H3)
nodes.statement: I have shown that $h_R(k[\varepsilon]) = Hom(R, k[\varepsilon]) \cong Der_\Lambda (R, k[\varepsilon]) \cong (\m_R / (\m_R ^ 2 + \m_\Lambda R))^*$. The main missing part is the linearity of the first bijection. The fact that $\m_R / (\m_R ^ 2 + \m_\Lambda R)$ is finite dimensional is also missing for now.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $h_R(k[\varepsilon])$ with derivations and the dual of $\m_R/(\m_R^2+\m_\Lambda R)$; linearity and finiteness still missing.

nodes.name: Linearity of Hom(k^r,k) -> Hom(k[k^r],k[epsilon])
nodes.statement: The map $Hom(k^r, k) \to Hom(k[k^r], k[\varepsilon])$ is $k$-linear ($r \in \N$). ($k$ here is the residue field of $\Lambda$)
assumptions: ($r \in \N$)
conclusions: The map $Hom(k^r, k) \to Hom(k[k^r], k[\varepsilon])$ is $k$-linear
nodes.label: lem:linearequiv_map

nodes.name: Fibre product of quotients
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a $Λ$-algebra, and $J, K$ ideals of $R$. Then, $$R / J \times_{R/(J + K)} R / K \cong R / (J \cap K)$$
assumptions: Let $R$ be a $Λ$-algebra, and $J, K$ ideals of $R$.
conclusions: $$R / J \times_{R/(J + K)} R / K \cong R / (J \cap K)$$
nodes.label: lem:quot_inf_equiv

nodes.name: Quotients of the power series ring are complete
nodes.statement: In the proof of the theorem, we have $r \in \N$, $S = \Lambda[[X_1, \cdots, X_r]]$, and $J \neq S$ an ideal of $S$. $S / J$ is complete (as a local ring).
assumptions: we have $r \in \N$, $S = \Lambda[[X_1, \cdots, X_r]]$, and $J \neq S$ an ideal of $S$.
conclusions: $S / J$ is complete (as a local ring).
nodes.label: lem:iscompletequot

nodes.name: Introduce $f$, $g$ and the fibre product set $P$
nodes.statement: Let $f : X \to Z$ and $g : Y \to Z$ be morphisms in $\CL$. Consider the set $P = \{(x, y) \in X \times Y ~\vert~ f (x) = g (y)\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $f$, $g$ and the fibre product set $P$

nodes.name: $\m_X \times \m_Y$ gives the maximal ideal of $P$
nodes.statement: Since $f$ and $g$ are local, the subset $\m_X \times \m_Y$ is an ideal (which is maximal).

nodes.name: Residue field of $P$ is $k$
nodes.statement: We have $\rf_\Lambda \to \rf_P \to \rf_X$, so $\rf_P \cong k$.

nodes.name: $P$ is Artinian via length lemma
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $X$ and $Y$ are Artinian $\Lambda$-modules by \cref{lem:lengtheq}, $P$ is an Artinian $\Lambda$-module as well, so it is an Artinian ring.

nodes.name: Length additivity and length lemma give (2)$\iff$(3)
nodes.statement: Since $p$ is surjective, we have $\length_\Lambda (B) = \length_\Lambda (A) + \length_\Lambda (\ker p)$, and we also have that $\length_B (\ker p) = 1$ if and only if $\ker p$ is a minimal non-zero ideal, so using \cref{lem:lengtheq} we get $(2) \iff (3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Length additivity and length lemma give (2)$\iff$(3)

nodes.name: Remains to show (1)$\iff$(2)
nodes.statement: We now show $(1) \iff (2)$.

nodes.name: (1)$\Rightarrow$(2): sub-ideals of $(t)$ vanish
nodes.statement: Assume that $p$ is a small extension, write $\ker p = (t)$, let $I < \ker p$ be an ideal and $x \in I$. There exists $y \in B$ such that $x = ty$. Since $I \ne (t)$, $y$ is not a unit, so we have $y \in \m_B$, and $x = 0$ by definition of a small extension. So $I=0$ and $\ker p$ is minimal.

nodes.name: (2)$\Rightarrow$(1): kernel principal and killed by $\m_B$
nodes.statement: Assume that $\ker p$ is a minimal non-zero ideal. Let $t \in \ker p \setminus \{0\}$. By minimality, we have $\ker p = (t)$. Furthermore, since $\m_B$ is nilpotent and $\ker p \neq 0$ we have $\m_B \cdot \ker p \neq \ker p$ so $\m_B \cdot \ker p = 0$ by minimality. So $p$ is a small extension.

nodes.name: Induction on the length of $B$
nodes.statement: By induction on $\length_\Lambda (B) \in \N$.

nodes.name: Base: zero kernel means isomorphism
nodes.statement: If $\ker p = 0$, then $p$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Pick a minimal non-zero ideal $I$
nodes.statement: Otherwise, there exists a minimal non-zero ideal $I$ of $B$ because $B$ is Artinian.

nodes.name: $p$ factors through the small extension $B \to B/I$
nodes.statement: By minimality, since $\ker p \neq 0$, we have $I \le \ker p$, so $p$ factorizes through the small extension $B \to B/I$.
nodes.statement_short: $p$ factors through the small extension $B \to B/I$

nodes.name: Apply induction hypothesis to $B/I \to A$
nodes.statement: We conclude by applying the induction hypothesis to the map $B/I \to A$.

nodes.name: Reduce to showing primes are maximal
nodes.statement: A Noetherian ring is Artinian if and only if it has Krull dimension 0, so it suffices to show that any prime ideal is maximal.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing primes are maximal

nodes.name: Nilpotent maximal ideal lies in every prime
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be a prime ideal. Since $\m^n = 0 \le I$ we have $\m \le I$, so $I = \m$ is maximal.
nodes.statement_short: Nilpotent maximal ideal lies in every prime

nodes.name: Introduce addition, scalar and zero maps
nodes.statement: Let $M \in \Mod_R^{fg}$. Write $s : M \times M \to M$ for the addition map, $\lambda_r : M \to M$ for the scalar multiplication by $r \in R$, and $z : 0 \to M$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce addition, scalar and zero maps

nodes.name: Push structure maps through $L$ and check axioms
nodes.statement: The module structure on $L(M)$ is defined using the images of these morphisms by $L$, together with the identification $L(M\times M) \cong L(M) \times L(M)$, and the fact that $L(0)$ is terminal in $Sets$ so it is a singleton. Checking that this defines a module structure is rather straightforward, by writing suitable commutative diagrams in $\Mod_R^{fg}$ and pushing them with $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Push structure maps through $L$ and check axioms

nodes.name: A section is not surjective by length
nodes.statement: If $p$ has a section $s$, then $p$ is not essential since $s$ is not surjective as we have $\length_\Lambda (B) = \length_\Lambda (A) + 1$.
nodes.statement_short: A section is not surjective by length

nodes.name: Assume non-essential with witness $q$
nodes.statement: Now, suppose that $p$ is not essential, and let $q : C \to B$ be such that $q \circ p$ is surjective but $q$ is not.

nodes.name: Length of the image $C'$ equals length of $A$
nodes.statement: Let $C'$ be the range of $q$. We have $\length_\Lambda (C') < \length_\Lambda (B)$ since $q$ is not surjective so $\length_\Lambda (C') \le \length_\Lambda (A)$, and $\length_\Lambda (C') \ge \length_\Lambda (A)$ because $p\restr{C'}$ is surjective (because $q \circ p$ is).
nodes.statement_short: Length of the image $C'$ equals length of $A$

nodes.name: Restriction is bijective, giving the section
nodes.statement: Thus $p\restr{C'}$ is bijective which gives the section that we wanted.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction is bijective, giving the section

nodes.name: Define the map
nodes.statement: It is given by $(x, r + y) \mapsto (x, x + y)$.

nodes.name: Explicit inverse
nodes.statement: The inverse map is $(x, y) \mapsto (x, x_0 + y - x)$ where $x_0$ is the $k$ residue of $x$. It is easy to check that this defines an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Reduce to $J_N \le J + \m_R^n$
nodes.statement: We need to show that for any $n \in \N$, there exists $N\in\N$ such that $J_N \le J + \m_R^n$.

nodes.name: Artinian quotients force stabilization
nodes.statement: For every $k \in \N$, $R / \m_R^k$ is Artinian, so the decreasing sequence $(J_i + \m_R^k)_{i \in \N}$ stabilizes.

nodes.name: Define stabilization indices $N_k$
nodes.statement: We write $N_k$ for some index such that $J_{N_k} + \m_R^k$ is the minimum of the sequence.

nodes.name: $J_{N_k} \le J_k$
nodes.statement: Note that we have $J_{N_k} + \m_R^k \le J_k + \m_R^k$ so since we also have $\m_R^k \le J_k$ we get that $J_{N_k} \le J_k$.

nodes.name: Claim $J_{N_n} \le J + \m_R^n$
nodes.statement: We claim that $J_{N_n} \le J + \m_R^n$. Let $x \in J_{N_n}$. We define a Cauchy sequence $(x_i)$ in $R$ with $x_i \in J_{N_i}$ for $i \ge n$ by induction, by first setting $x_i = x$ if $i \le n$. If $i > n$, then there exists $x_{i+1} \in J_{N_{i+1}}$ such that $x_i - x_{i+1} \in \m_R ^ i$: indeed if $N_{i+1} \le N_i$ we can take $x_{i+1}= x_i$, and otherwise we have $J_{N_{i+1}} + \m_R^i = J_{N_i} + \m_R^i$ (note that have $x_i \in J_{N_i}$). Since $R$ is complete, this sequence admits a limit $y$. We have $y \in J_{N_i} + \m_R^i$ for all $i$ so $y \in J$ and $y - x = y - x_n \in \m_R ^ n$, so $x \in J + \m_R^n$.

nodes.name: Start a Cauchy sequence at $x$
nodes.statement: Let $x \in J_{N_n}$. We define a Cauchy sequence $(x_i)$ in $R$ with $x_i \in J_{N_i}$ for $i \ge n$ by induction, by first setting $x_i = x$ if $i \le n$.

nodes.name: Inductive construction of $x_{i+1}$
nodes.statement: If $i > n$, then there exists $x_{i+1} \in J_{N_{i+1}}$ such that $x_i - x_{i+1} \in \m_R ^ i$: indeed if $N_{i+1} \le N_i$ we can take $x_{i+1}= x_i$, and otherwise we have $J_{N_{i+1}} + \m_R^i = J_{N_i} + \m_R^i$ (note that have $x_i \in J_{N_i}$).

nodes.name: Completeness gives a limit $y$
nodes.statement: Since $R$ is complete, this sequence admits a limit $y$.

nodes.name: $y \in J$ and $x - y \in \m_R^n$
nodes.statement: We have $y \in J_{N_i} + \m_R^i$ for all $i$ so $y \in J$ and $y - x = y - x_n \in \m_R ^ n$, so $x \in J + \m_R^n$.

nodes.name: Assume (H1)-(H3); set $r$, $S$, $\n$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$ and $(H_3)$. Let $r = \dim_k(t_F)$, $S = \Lambda[[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]$ and $\n$ the maximal ideal of $S$.

nodes.name: Plan: inductive sequence $(J_q,\xi_q)$
nodes.statement: We first construct $R$ as a projective limit of quotients of $S$. More specifically we define a sequence $(J_q, \xi_q)_{q\ge2}$ by induction where $(J_q)$ is a decreasing sequence of ideals of $S$ such that $R_q = S / J_q \in \CL$ and $\xi_q \in F(R_q)$ is such that $(\xi_q) \in \varprojlim F(R_q)$.

nodes.name: Base ideal $J_2$
nodes.statement: First we set $J_2 = \n^2 + \m_\Lambda S$ and $R_2 = S/J_2$.

nodes.name: Construct $\xi_2$ via (H2) and a basis of $t_F$
nodes.statement: There exists $\xi_2 \in R_2$ inducing an isomorphism $\Hom (R_2, k[\varepsilon]) \cong t_F$. To see this, first note that $R_2 \cong k[k^r] \cong k[\varepsilon]^r$. By applying $(H_2)$, this yields $F(R_2) \cong t_F^r$, so choosing a basis $(e_1, \ldots, e_r)$ of $t_F$ gives an element $\xi_2 \in F(R_2)$. We then check that $u \mapsto F(u)(\xi_2)$ is an isomorphism. In fact, this map is linear and sends the morphism $R_2 \to k[\varepsilon]$ corresponding to the $i$-th projection $k^r \to k$ to $e_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\xi_2$ via (H2) and a basis of $t_F$

nodes.name: Claim existence of $\xi_2$
nodes.statement: There exists $\xi_2 \in R_2$ inducing an isomorphism $\Hom (R_2, k[\varepsilon]) \cong t_F$.

nodes.name: $R_2 \cong k[\varepsilon]^r$
nodes.statement: To see this, first note that $R_2 \cong k[k^r] \cong k[\varepsilon]^r$.

nodes.name: (H2) gives $F(R_2) \cong t_F^r$; choose basis
nodes.statement: By applying $(H_2)$, this yields $F(R_2) \cong t_F^r$, so choosing a basis $(e_1, \ldots, e_r)$ of $t_F$ gives an element $\xi_2 \in F(R_2)$.

nodes.name: The induced map is a linear isomorphism
nodes.statement: We then check that $u \mapsto F(u)(\xi_2)$ is an isomorphism. In fact, this map is linear and sends the morphism $R_2 \to k[\varepsilon]$ corresponding to the $i$-th projection $k^r \to k$ to $e_i$.
nodes.statement_short: The induced map is a linear isomorphism

nodes.name: Inductive step: the set $\mathscr{S}$ of admissible ideals
nodes.statement: For the induction step, suppose that we have an ideal $J_q$ such that $R_q = S/J_q \in \CL$ and $\xi_q \in F(R_q)$. Consider the set $\mathscr{S}$ of ideals $J$ of $S$ such that $\n J_q \le J \le J_q$ and $\xi_q$ lifts to $F(S/J)$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: the set $\mathscr{S}$ of admissible ideals

nodes.name: $\mathscr{S}$ has a minimum
nodes.statement: We will set $J_{q+1}$ to be the minimum of $\mathscr{S}$, with $\xi_{q+1}$ some lift of $\xi_q$, after proving that it exists. First note that $\mathscr{S}$ is not empty as it contains $J_q$, and since $S / \n J_q$ is Artinian, we know that $\mathscr{S}$ admits a minimal element, so we only need to show that $\mathscr{S}$ is stable by pairwise intersection to get a minimum. Let $J$ and $K$ be two elements of $\mathscr{S}$. The elements of $\mathscr{S}$ are in correspondence with $k$-vector subspaces of $J/\n J_q$, so we can extend $J$ into some ideal $J' \le J_q$ such that $J' \cap K = J \cap K$ and $J' + K = J_q$, and we have $J' \in \mathscr{S}$ because $J \le J'$. We now use the isomorphism $$S/J' \times_{S/J_q} S/K \cong S/(J \cap K)$$ together with \cref{lem:h1+} to conclude that $\xi_q$ lifts to $S/(J \cap K)$, i.e. that $J \cap K \in \mathscr{S}$, which concludes the induction step.

nodes.name: Define $J_{q+1}$ as minimum of $\mathscr{S}$
nodes.statement: We will set $J_{q+1}$ to be the minimum of $\mathscr{S}$, with $\xi_{q+1}$ some lift of $\xi_q$, after proving that it exists.

nodes.name: Reduce to stability under intersection
nodes.statement: First note that $\mathscr{S}$ is not empty as it contains $J_q$, and since $S / \n J_q$ is Artinian, we know that $\mathscr{S}$ admits a minimal element, so we only need to show that $\mathscr{S}$ is stable by pairwise intersection to get a minimum.

nodes.name: Enlarge $J$ to $J'$ with $J' + K = J_q$
nodes.statement: Let $J$ and $K$ be two elements of $\mathscr{S}$. The elements of $\mathscr{S}$ are in correspondence with $k$-vector subspaces of $J/\n J_q$, so we can extend $J$ into some ideal $J' \le J_q$ such that $J' \cap K = J \cap K$ and $J' + K = J_q$, and we have $J' \in \mathscr{S}$ because $J \le J'$.

nodes.name: Fibre product of quotients plus (H1) extension lift $\xi_q$
nodes.statement: We now use the isomorphism $$S/J' \times_{S/J_q} S/K \cong S/(J \cap K)$$ together with \cref{lem:h1+} to conclude that $\xi_q$ lifts to $S/(J \cap K)$, i.e. that $J \cap K \in \mathscr{S}$, which concludes the induction step.
nodes.statement_short: Fibre product of quotients plus (H1) extension lift $\xi_q$

nodes.name: Define $R$ and $\xi$ as limits
nodes.statement: We set $J = \bigcap_{q \ge 2} J_q$ and $R = S / J$. By definition of the $J_q$'s, we have $\n ^ q \le J_q$, so \cref{lem:topo} applies and $\hat{F}(R) = \varprojlim F(S/J_q)$, so we can set $\xi = \varprojlim \xi_q \in \hat{F}(R)$.

nodes.name: Tangent spaces agree
nodes.statement: We have $\Hom (R, k[\varepsilon]) \cong \Hom (R_2, k[\varepsilon])$ because any map $S \to k[\varepsilon]$ factorizes through $S/J_2$, and since $\xi$ projects to $\xi_2$ we have $t_R \cong t_F$ by definition of $\xi_2$.

nodes.name: Remains: smoothness
nodes.statement: It remains to show that $\nattrans(\xi) : h_R \to F$ is smooth.

nodes.name: Reduce smoothness to small extension lifting problem
nodes.statement: Using \cref{lem:smoothsmallext}, let $p : A' \to A$ be a small extension, $u : R \to A$, $\eta' \in F(A')$ and $\eta \in F(A)$ such that $\nattrans(\xi) (u) = F(p)(\eta') = \eta$. We need to find $u' : R \to A'$ such that $\nattrans(\xi) (u') = \eta'$ and $p \circ u' = u$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce smoothness to small extension lifting problem

nodes.name: Reduce to lifting $u$ via the transitive action
nodes.statement: First we reduce this to finding $u'' : R \to A'$ such that $p \circ u'' = u$. Indeed, if we have such a $u''$, then $\nattrans(\xi) (u'')$ and $\eta'$ both lie over $\eta$, so by \cref{lem:actionH1}, there exists $\sigma \in F(k[I])$ sending $\nattrans(\xi) (u'')$ to $\eta'$, where $I = \ker p$. By using \cref{lem:actionnattrans} and the fact that $h_R (k[I]) \cong F(k[I])$ (using \cref{lem:vsnatiso}), we can also apply $\sigma$ to $u''$ giving us the $u' : R \to A'$ that we wanted.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to lifting $u$ via the transitive action

nodes.name: Reduce to any lift $u''$
nodes.statement: First we reduce this to finding $u'' : R \to A'$ such that $p \circ u'' = u$.

nodes.name: (H1) action gives $\sigma$
nodes.statement: Indeed, if we have such a $u''$, then $\nattrans(\xi) (u'')$ and $\eta'$ both lie over $\eta$, so by \cref{lem:actionH1}, there exists $\sigma \in F(k[I])$ sending $\nattrans(\xi) (u'')$ to $\eta'$, where $I = \ker p$.

nodes.name: Transport $\sigma$ to $h_R$
nodes.statement: By using \cref{lem:actionnattrans} and the fact that $h_R (k[I]) \cong F(k[I])$ (using \cref{lem:vsnatiso}), we can also apply $\sigma$ to $u''$ giving us the $u' : R \to A'$ that we wanted.

nodes.name: Build the lift $v$ via essential small extensions
nodes.statement: Since $u$ factorizes through $R/\m_R^n \to A$ for some $n$, and the topology is induced by the $J_q$'s (\cref{lem:topo}), $u$ factorizes through $R_q \to A$ for some $q$. It suffices to find $v$ completing the following diagram: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} S \arrow[rr, "w"] \arrow[d] & & R_q \times_A A' \arrow[d, "pr_1"] \\ R_{q+1} \arrow[rr] \arrow[rru, "v", dashed] & & R_q \end{tikzcd} \end{center} where $w$ is defined using the universal property of $S = \Lambda [[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]$ to make the diagram commute. More specifically, to define $w$ we use that $pr_1$ is surjective so that we can first define $w$ on the $X_i$'s, and since all maps are local the images of the $X_i$'s are in the maximal ideal so we can extend the map to $S$. In this context we can easily show that $pr_1$ is a small extension, so we can apply \cref{lem:14ii}. If $pr_1$ admits a section then we are done. Otherwise, $pr_1$ is essential, and $pr_1 \circ w$ is the quotient map $S \to R_q$, so $w$ is surjective by \cref{lem:essential_proartin}. By $(H_1)$, $\xi_q$ lifts to $R_q \times_A A'$, so $\ker w \in \mathscr{S}$ and by minimality we have $J_{q+1} \le \ker w$. Thus $w$ factors through $R_{q+1}$ giving the $v$ that we wanted.
nodes.statement_short: Build the lift $v$ via essential small extensions

nodes.name: $u$ factors through some $R_q$
nodes.statement: Since $u$ factorizes through $R/\m_R^n \to A$ for some $n$, and the topology is induced by the $J_q$'s (\cref{lem:topo}), $u$ factorizes through $R_q \to A$ for some $q$.

nodes.name: Reduce to completing a diagram, with $w$ from the universal
nodes.statement: It suffices to find $v$ completing the following diagram: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} S \arrow[rr, "w"] \arrow[d] & & R_q \times_A A' \arrow[d, "pr_1"] \\ R_{q+1} \arrow[rr] \arrow[rru, "v", dashed] & & R_q \end{tikzcd} \end{center} where $w$ is defined using the universal property of $S = \Lambda [[X_1, \ldots, X_r]]$ to make the diagram commute. More specifically, to define $w$ we use that $pr_1$ is surjective so that we can first define $w$ on the $X_i$'s, and since all maps are local the images of the $X_i$'s are in the maximal ideal so we can extend the map to $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to completing a diagram, with $w$ from the universal property of $S$

nodes.name: $pr_1$ is a small extension; apply split criterion
nodes.statement: In this context we can easily show that $pr_1$ is a small extension, so we can apply \cref{lem:14ii}.
nodes.statement_short: $pr_1$ is a small extension; apply split criterion

nodes.name: Section case or essential case: $w$ surjective
nodes.statement: If $pr_1$ admits a section then we are done. Otherwise, $pr_1$ is essential, and $pr_1 \circ w$ is the quotient map $S \to R_q$, so $w$ is surjective by \cref{lem:essential_proartin}.
nodes.statement_short: Section case or essential case: $w$ surjective

nodes.name: Minimality of $J_{q+1}$ gives $v$
nodes.statement: By $(H_1)$, $\xi_q$ lifts to $R_q \times_A A'$, so $\ker w \in \mathscr{S}$ and by minimality we have $J_{q+1} \le \ker w$. Thus $w$ factors through $R_{q+1}$ giving the $v$ that we wanted.

nodes.name: Assume a hull $(R,\xi)$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $F$ admits a hull $(R, \xi)$.

nodes.name: (H3) transfers from $h_R$
nodes.statement: First since $t_R \cong t_F$ (linearly by \cref{lem:vsnatlin}), and $h_R$ satisfies $(H_3)$, $F$ satisfies $(H_3)$.

nodes.name: (H1) via smooth lifting
nodes.statement:
To check $(H_1)$, let $f : X 	o Z$ and $g : Y 	o Z$ be morphisms in $\CL$ with $g$ surjective, and $x \in F(X)$ and $y \in F(Y)$ both lying over $z \in F(Z)$. First, since $h_R 	o F$ is smooth, by \cref{lem:surj_of_smooth} there exists $u_x : R 	o X$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u_x) = x$. Then by smoothness applied to $g$, there exists $u_y : R 	o Y$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u_y) = y$ and $g \circ u_y = f \circ u_x$. Then $
attrans(\xi)(u_x 	imes u_y) \in F(X 	imes_Z Y)$ projects to $x$ and $y$, so $p_{f, g}$ is surjective.

nodes.name: Set up $f$, $g$, $x$, $y$
nodes.statement: To check $(H_1)$, let $f : X \to Z$ and $g : Y \to Z$ be morphisms in $\CL$ with $g$ surjective, and $x \in F(X)$ and $y \in F(Y)$ both lying over $z \in F(Z)$.

nodes.name: Lift $x$ to $u_x$
nodes.statement: First, since $h_R \to F$ is smooth, by \cref{lem:surj_of_smooth} there exists $u_x : R \to X$ such that $\nattrans(\xi) (u_x) = x$.

nodes.name: Lift $y$ compatibly to $u_y$
nodes.statement: Then by smoothness applied to $g$, there exists $u_y : R \to Y$ such that $\nattrans(\xi) (u_y) = y$ and $g \circ u_y = f \circ u_x$.

nodes.name: Product map gives preimage
nodes.statement: Then $\nattrans(\xi)(u_x \times u_y) \in F(X \times_Z Y)$ projects to $x$ and $y$, so $p_{f, g}$ is surjective.

nodes.name: (H2): injectivity via tangent isomorphism
nodes.statement:
To check $(H_2)$, we now only need to check injectivity, since we have already shown $(H_1)$. Let $A \in \CL$ and $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ in $F(A 	imes k[\varepsilon])$ having the same projections $a \in F(A)$ and $e \in k[\varepsilon]$. We proceed similarly as in the proof of $(H_1)$. First there is $u' : R 	o A$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u') = a$. Then by smoothness applied to the projection $pr_1 : A 	imes k[\varepsilon] 	o A$, we get maps $u_i : R 	o A 	imes k[\varepsilon]$ for $i = 1, 2$ such that $
attrans(\xi) (u_i) = \zeta_i$ and $pr_1 \circ u_i = u'$. Since $
attrans(\xi) (pr_2 \circ u_i) = e$ in both cases, and $
attrans(\xi)_{k[\varepsilon]}$ is an isomorphism, we have $u_1 = u_2$ so $\zeta_1 = \zeta_2$.

nodes.name: Only injectivity remains
nodes.statement: To check $(H_2)$, we now only need to check injectivity, since we have already shown $(H_1)$.

nodes.name: Set up $\zeta_1$, $\zeta_2$
nodes.statement: Let $A \in \CL$ and $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ in $F(A \times k[\varepsilon])$ having the same projections $a \in F(A)$ and $e \in k[\varepsilon]$. We proceed similarly as in the proof of $(H_1)$.

nodes.name: Smooth lifts $u_1$, $u_2$
nodes.statement: First there is $u' : R \to A$ such that $\nattrans(\xi) (u') = a$. Then by smoothness applied to the projection $pr_1 : A \times k[\varepsilon] \to A$, we get maps $u_i : R \to A \times k[\varepsilon]$ for $i = 1, 2$ such that $\nattrans(\xi) (u_i) = \zeta_i$ and $pr_1 \circ u_i = u'$.

nodes.name: Tangent isomorphism forces $u_1 = u_2$
nodes.statement: Since $\nattrans(\xi) (pr_2 \circ u_i) = e$ in both cases, and $\nattrans(\xi)_{k[\varepsilon]}$ is an isomorphism, we have $u_1 = u_2$ so $\zeta_1 = \zeta_2$.

nodes.name: Assume (H1)-(H4)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $F$ satisfies $(H_1)$, $(H_2)$, $(H_3)$ and $(H_4)$.

nodes.name: Existence of a hull
nodes.statement: By the first point of the theorem, we know that $F$ admits a hull $(R, \xi)$.

nodes.name: Surjectivity from smoothness
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $\nattrans(\xi)$ is smooth, we already know that $\nattrans(\xi)_A$ is surjective for all $A \in \CL$ (\cref{lem:surj_of_smooth}).

nodes.name: Induction on length for injectivity
nodes.statement: We will show by induction on $\length_\Lambda (A)$ that it is injective, using \cref{lem:smallextexist}.

nodes.name: Base case $A = k$
nodes.statement: If $A = k$, then this is true by definition of a hull.

nodes.name: Inductive step on a small extension
nodes.statement: Otherwise, let $p : B \to A$ be a small extension, with $I = \ker p$, and suppose that $\nattrans(\xi)_A$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step on a small extension

nodes.name: (H4) action and functoriality give injectivity
nodes.statement: By applying \cref{lem:actionH4} together with \cref{lem:actionnattrans}, it is easy check that $\nattrans(\xi)_B$ is injective.

nodes.name: Zero action sends $u_1$ to $u_2$
nodes.statement: Namely we take $u_1$ and $u_2$ in $h_R(B)$ such that $\nattrans(\xi) (u_1) = \nattrans(\xi) (u_2)$, and we need to show that the action of $h_R(k[I])$ by $0$ sends $u_1$ to $u_2$, which is clear from the commutative diagram in \cref{lem:actionnattrans}.
